Your children will most readily acquire

Your safeguard against being imposed upon
by words of good omen, used as a screen for
indifferent or bad practice, is to bear steadily
in mind what (giving no heed to words and
sounds) you are in search of, You wish to see
your children grow up to be instructed, capable
and well-conducted men and women. You
feel yourselves to be unequal, without aid, to
do all that is desirable for the purpose. Doing
your own part, to the best of your ability, you
seek aid, at least, in technical instruction.
Sad will it be, if aid, for the sake of technical

If you can succeed in finding the right kind

efforts and their assistance, your children
should eventually start' from school and
home—gifted with fair earning powers, and
with habits and dispositions. inclining them to

will be amply rewarded, and will deserve and
receive their affectionate gratitude.
One more remark, and I have dorm. Your
children are destined to mix in society, such as

Their education will have prepared them to
share in the good and cope with: the evil.
But you can do yet a little more to sweeten

vice, which still prevail are mainly the conse-
quence of former parental neglect. And there
are children now growing up, side by eitle

similar neglect—to be wretched in themselves,
and. sources of annoyance and torment to
your own children. You have probably quite
enough to do directly in providing for your
own children. But, indirectly, through
tho Government, through your parish and
board of education, you may exercise a most
useful influence in procuring for these
neglected ones, not merely school-room, but
teachers who, in the name of education, will
gift their pupils with fair earning powers, and
with habits and dispositions so to use their
earnings, as to preserve them from want and
its consequent temptations.

EDUCATION.

HINTS FOR PARENTS REGARDING TILE FUTURE

OF THEIR CHILDREN.

IT is well known to you that there is a wide
feeling of discontent at the miserable condition
of largo masse p of the inhabitants of this
country. Some people try to console us by
directing our attention to the greater misery
which prevails in other countries. The cor-
rectness of this representation is, however,
often disputed by others. But whether it be
well or ill-founded, our interest in obtaining
some amendment of our condition is none the
less. If well-founded, it should not lead us to
relax our efforts, but only warn us to be care-
ful not to drift into a worse condition while
attempting to improve the present.
The proofs on which the sufferers and those
who sympathise with them ground their com-
plaints are notorious, even if they do not
justify the language in which the complaints
are sometimes expressed. Here are the heads
of a few of them :

Wages inadequate to sustain decent exist-
ence;
Unwholesome and over-crowded dwellings;
Insufficient food and clothing;
Short allowance of recreation and other en-
joyments needful for health;
Lack of medical and nursing attendance in
illness.

A statement, even given in detail, of the
grievances complained of would be incomplete
ii not accompanied by some notice of the means
through which the sufferers and their advisers
are hoping to obtain relief. These may be
accepted as samples :
Co-operation ; Emigration; Unions or Com-
binations, with or without strikes; 'Repeal of
Taxes; Protection and other safe-guards
against competition; not to mention the Go-
vernment assistance, so often invoked in a
variety of forms.
Such is the state of society and of public
opinion in which your children are born ;
themselves, in the beginning, feeble, ignorant,
and incapable, looking to you for sustenance,
guidance, and instruction. You are desirous
to see them healthy and cheerful, while under
your protection, and to feel assured that after-
wards they will be able to take care of them-
selves.

Are your children, as they approach man-
hood, to take rank among the discontented and
suffering, or among the contented and comfort-
able classes? Will, your efforts on behalf of
your own children succeed hi diminishing the
number of the discontented, as compared with
that of the contented?

You will not, I am sure, turn aside from
these as idle questions. Nor can you be indif-
ferent to the answers which will be given to
them, and to the line of conduct which the
answers will point to.
It would be out of place hero to offer any
opinion upon the expediency or efficacy of any
of the plans for improving the condition of
society to which I have referred. Excellent
as they may be, or otherwise, they must bo
accompanied by something besides, or the
future condition of society can hardly be
expected to differ greatly from what it now is.
To this "something besides" I would now
call your attention. I might mislead you, or
cause you to understand one thing while I
mean another, if I were to content myself with
giving this " something " a name. With your
leave, therefore, I will preface the name with
a few words of explanation.
No thoughtful man can hesitate to admit
that a state of society will be favourable or the
reverse, according as the individuals which
compose it are industrious, intelligent., skil-
ful, thrifty, sober, trustworthy, orderly, tria t h
, persevering, courageous, forbearing, and
humane; anxious to learn and know their
duties and conscientious in performing them.
The prospect for your children of sharing in the
actual well-being of society, whatever that
may be, will, of course, greatly depend upon
the extent to which they share in the qualities
conducive to well-being.

You need not be cautioned that each indi-
vidual's share in the general well-being is not
to be estimated by the share to which he
attains in the general wealth. Since although
sufficiency of wealth for the purposes of health
and comfort is indispensable for well-being,
the possession of wealth in addition is much
less conducive to well-being than the habits
and intelligence which determine the uses of
wealth after it has been acquired.
If, then, it be beyond dispute that you can
have no hope either for the improvement of
society or for the well-being of your
.chil-
dren, except so far as you can assist in gifting
them with the qualities which lead to well-
being, these questions are forced upon you :
What can we do ? What ought we to do?
There is one answer which you cannot fail
to give and also to receive from others. You
must educate your children. And to make
education efficient for the purposes mentioned,
you yourselves must educate your own chil-
dren. Be it understood, you must avail your-
selves of the assistance of others, as you do for
all the other purposes of life, for the feeding,
clothing, and lodging of yourselves and chil-
dren. You must seek the assistance of schools
and teachers. But they are to supplement,
not to supersede, your own work and influence.
They may be mighty in what they superadd to
the discipline and example of home; and they
may mitigate iii some measure the lack or the
misdirection of parental care. No school in-
fluence can compensate for the absenee of good
home influence.

The stage to which society has advanced
almost precludes the possibility of conducting
education without the aid of schools and ex-
perienced teachers. There is so much to be
learned and practised and prepared for to
qualify each individual to occupy a place in
society with comfort to himself and usefulness
to others. But while parents, anxious for the
welfare of their children, feel that they need
the co-operation of others, they must seek with
their eyes open. The word " cducatiun " is,

THE DOUBLE-SHIFT SYSTEM.

Mn. HARRISON is an able and most vigorou
writer; but the double-shift system pro.
pounded by him in the Fortnightly _Review
will not hold water. He suggests it as a
panacea, by which the interests of capital and
labour might be completely reconciled—a
a mode of production by which the labourer
would only have to work eight hours a day,
being paid the same as when he worked ten,
and by which the employer would have the
same profits as before; that is to say, when. the
hands worked ten hours.

Mr. HARRISON'S double-shift system, if
carried out, would require the manufactory
and workshops to be kept open eighteen hours
a dig at least, winter as well as summer. The
manner in which it would be carried on would
be this: The men of the first shift would get
up, say, at five o'clock in the morning, break-
fast, and commence work at six. They would
then continue work till ten—four hours—leave
off work for an hour, commence work at eleven
and leave off at three. So much, for the first
shift. The second shift would commence at
three, work till seven, leave off fOr an hour,
recommence at eight, and finish at midnight.
Such is Mr. HARRISON'S double-shift system.
Now compare it with the single-shift system of
eight hours, which I suggested in the BRE-
HIVE a fortnight ago. According to my plan,
the labourer would commence work at eight
summer and winter, after breakfasting, would
leave off at twelve for an hour, during which
period he would lunch or dine. At one he
would recommence work, and leave off finally
at five, thus completing his eight hours of
labour, without being obliged to rise earlier than
seven—having the whole evening, from five
till bed-time, entirely to himself. I appeal to
the readers of the Bee-fIlvE belonging to the
working class if they would not, one ancl:
all, infinitely prefer my system of*, a;
single shift of eight hours to Mr. EfauntsoN's
double-shift system. Mr. HARRISON assumes,
however, in his article in the Fortnightly
Review, that the employer would consent to
his hands working only eight hours instead of
ten, provided the double-shift system was
carried out. 13-at upon what ground does Mr.
HARRISON adopt such an assumption ? In what
would the capitalist be benefited by employing
one.half of his workmen during eight hours
and the other half eight hours additional
when the first shift had finished ? Would it
not be better for him, OS well as for his
labourers, to do the whole work at one shift
the middle of the day ?

TRADE UNIONISNI AND OUR /:ORq(3ISI

TRADE.

Ti• E false prophets who predicted at the
time that an increase of wages and reduation
of the hours of labour took place in certain
branches of industry that our foreign trade
would be ruined by the action of trades unions,
have been greatly at fault. The Board of
Trade returns for the first nine months of this
year ending September 30th, show our ex-
ports 0 be £100,31.5,000 against• £165,677,000
for the same period last year, being an increase
of £21,788,000 on the first nine months. Now
these figures alone are an. answer to all the
jargon and nonsense whin!' certain writers and
pseudo-political economists trumpet forth to
the public to frighten timid people out of their
wits.

It would be information worth having if
there were any means of aseertaiaing what
amount of profit merehants, manufacturers,
stud capitalists in general, have derived from
the production of this vast wealth.
Mr. TIIOIIAS BRIO", in a paper which he
road at the Social Science Congress, and. which
appeart4 in the BEE-HIVE on the 12th lust.,
has a fling at trades uniens in this reaped, in
a very singular way. Mr. Ilittoos says—" To
say that the strong shall be brought down to
the level of the weak,is as great an absurdity
as to say that the weak shall be lifted. up to the
level of the strong. It is very like finding
fault with the CREAM'S work, and. pretend-
ing to correct it. And yet it is this our trades
unions are trying to do," Is it indeed Where
in the world did Mr.BRIGGS learn this
have been a trades unionist for more thau 30
years, and I have never seen any attempt or
desire upon the part of trades unionists to
" try " and establish the kind of equality Mr.
BRIGGIS alludes to, nor to wino) an uncondi-
tional uniform rate of wages.
I speak both as a trades unionist and an
employer of labour, havingemployed thousands
of men during thnlast twenty years in most of
the principal towns and districts in England
and Wales, and at the present time in three of
the principal centres of industry; and I never
hear or see any attempt upon the pert of these
mea to bring the strong Man "down to the
level of the weak," nor to lift up " the weak
meal to the level of the strong," if by that it
Ls meant that they should all ho pittoed on
equality in point of remuneration. I find it
. ,
much the Earie io* an it vraa before 1 lsit Ulf

workshop in that respect, namely, that a fair
average wage is expected to be paid to fair
average workmen, but I have never seen any
hard and fast line laid down that all men shall
be placed on equality and paid alike. If this
_ were so I should be amongst the first
to strike against it. My experience among
workmen has shown me that they have a far
better way of settling their claims to remunera-
tion than by demanding an unconditional
equality of pay. I have generally found that
where a workman is worth his salt and is
offered less wages than his neighbour, and
thinks he is slighted, he generally takes his
labour to another market, whore his abilities
are better appreciated and his services better
rewarded. This may not be a very satisfactory
or just way towards the workman of settling
the wage question, but at any rate it disposes
of the charge of pulling down the strong to the
"level of the weak," or lifting up the "weak
man to the level of the strong."
But if trades unions do not lift the "weak
man up to the level of the strong" in point of
equality of pay, these unions, at all events,
lift him up towards the "level of the strong "
in other ways. They render him succour and
:4upport when he is out of employment, when
ho is in ill-health, when accident or misfortune
overtakes him, or when death puts a period to
his existence ho is provided with the means of
decent burial. In all this good and noble
work trades unions spend tens of thousands
annually in "lifting up the weak towards the
strong." But they never got much credit for
all this ,goodlwork. They may save the pay-
ment of poor-Pates, and make the most praise- ,
worthy efflrts to lift up the weak to the level
of the strong" in this way, but very little
credit is given them for it. If, however, they
approach King Capital while his side pockets
are overflowing with gains, and he is widening
out and waxing largo from the fruits of their
industry, and ask his majesty to consider their
claims in his prosperity, the chances are that
they will be charged with a desire to "pull
down the strong man to the level of the weak,'
or drive trade from the country.
• Mr. Bnraas then goes on to say that "if
trades unions know how to state their case
properly they would be invincible. They
complain of injustice. In that they are quite
right, but they are very ignorant; they commit
a much greater injustice against themselves
and others than that of which they complain.
Being born with a constitution and physical
and mental powers of some sort, and having
no other property, they are obliged to work for
wages; that is, to let themselves out for
hire ; but the -laws (fiscal laws) in which
they have had no voice in the making,
take away from them at least one-third
of their wages, or what is the same thing,
make them pay in that proportion an in-
creased price for all that is necessary for their
existence in eating, drinking, clothing, and
housing." Now if we gather anything at all
from the foregoing statement, it is that trades
unions ought to strike against the "fiscal la "
which "takes away from them at least one-
third of their wages." There cannot be the
slightest doubt but what every trades unionist
will endorse that sentiment, and, in fact, many
of the leading trades unionists have, to my
certain knowledge, been working hard for fiscal
reform and a "free breakfast table" for
years, and I believe are prepared to work on
until that be accomplished. But Mr. Brims
does not quite understand these men if he
imagines that they are so "very ignorant"
that they do not know ‘` how to state their
case properly." They have stated their case
repeatedly, and will doubtless be prepared to
state it again in due season.
Mr. BRIGGS must know that trades unions
are not political organizations, nor are they
fiscal or financial reform associations, although
nearly all their leaders are very able, political,
fiscal, and financial reformers. Trades unions
Propose to deal chiefly with certain abuses
that crop up from time to time, and regulations
that require to be made between employers
and employed. And experience has taught
them that it is not the " fiscal laws " alone
" which take away from them at least one-
third of their wages," but that unscrupulous
employers oc3asionally take unto themselves
-a very large and savoury slice from "what is

necessary to their existence in eating, drink-
ing, clothing, &c."
But I rather suspect that the main object
Mr. BRIGGS has in view in his fling at trades
unions, is to convince them that high wages
are detrimental to the trade, commerce, and
industry of the country. That is merely the
old see-saw jargon, which has been successfully
answered fifty times. No doubt if the price of
labour was run up to an exorbitant degree in
one country without any corresponding rise in
other countries, and at the same time weighted
with heavy taxation, there_ would be some
show of reason for the statement. But the
fact is, that in nearly all continental countries
the wages have risen as well as in England.
Moreover, we must settle first of all what is in
reality a high rate of wages, taking into
account their purchasing power? In addition
to this, the still more important question must
be answered, as to whether a high rate of
profits to manufacturers, merchants, and
capitalists in general, is not a vast deal more
detrimental to the trade, commerce, and
industry of a nation, than a high rate of wages.
The profits to capitalists this year have been
enormous. Let us take two branches of
industry for example. It is stated, upon the
most reliable authority, that the profits to the
coal and iron masters of this country will
exceed by £50,000,000 sterling the profits of
any former year, in consequence of their having
increased the price of coal and iron from 50 to
100 per cent., while the wages of their work-
men have not been raised more than from 20
to 30 per cent.
Nobody knows better than the capitalists
and employers of labour in this country, that
with the immense advantages which they possess
over every other country on the face of the
globe, in the shape of skilled robust labour,
coupled with the enormous amount of me-
chanical power at their command, together with
the inexhaustible supply of the raw materials
of coal and iron, they can compete successfully
with all the nations of the earth, secure large
profits to themselves, and give liberal wages
to their workmen also if they will: And seeing
the vast increase of wealth which has taken
place of late years, there does not seem any
reason why the producers of this vast increase
of wealth should not in some measure partici-
pate in a reasonable share of it. With regard
to the immense increase in wealth, Mr. GLAD-
STONE stated a short time ago in his speech at
Whitby, based upon official documents, that
whereas "the population had, during the last
35 to 40 years, increased at about the rate of
25 per cent., the wealth of the country had
increased 400 per cent." Now this is a most
important and reliable statement, and the
question which the producers of all this wealth
have to ask themselves, is, have they had any-
thing like a fair and reasonable share of this
immense increase
.of wealth they have pro-
duced?

A few words more upon the supposed
high rate of wages and I have done. Wages
may seem to be high when in reality from
their depreciated purchasing power they will
be nothing of the kind. And that is exactly
the ease at the present time. We all know
that the common necessaries of life have risen
greatly in price lately. And when a corre-
sponding rise in wages is asked for to meet
this, the working men are met with the state-
ment that the trade of the country will not
allow it, and they are not unfrequently
Visited with the wrath of their employers. I
saw a remarkable instance of this the other
day in my own neighbourhood, of a country
esquire and a "gentleman farmer," who upon
being asked for a rise in the miserable low
wages that he paid to his labourers, gave them
a rise with a vengence, but that rise happened
to be to tell them to rise, take up their beds,
and walk off his estate. These poor fellows
have no union among them, but it is just
possible that some day they may hear of Mr.
JOEPIE ARM. Now this is exactly the kind
of rise the mechanics and artizans would get
were it not for the moral and material power
of their unions; therefore I urge them never
to let go the anchor of unionism, but at the
same time to help Mr. Thatoos to get rid of
those "fiscal laws" which "takes away from
them one-third of their wages," and above all
to send men from their own rank to Parliament
to
‘assist to do it. ALFRED A. WALTON.

articles.text:
HANLEY.

THE NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE MINERS.

A deputation of miners waited upon the North
Staffordshire mine owners on Wednesday after-
noon, and asked for a further advance of 16 per
cont. in wages, and an allowance of 4 cwt. of
coal per man weekly. The employers stated that
in the present condition of trade they could not
make any advance. It is understood that the
men will acquiesce in the refusal.

articles.title: WOLVERHAMPTON.
articles.text:
WOLVERHAMPTON.

THE IRONWORKERS' UNION.

On Tuesday there was a great meeting of malle-
able ironworkers in Wolverhampton, at which it
was stated that their numbers were increasing at
the rate of 3,000 a month, that, as well as the men
in the north and the majority in the midlands, all
ihe ironworkers in South Wales were unionists,
and that, by the close of this month, they should
number upwards of 30,000 members. Efforts were
being made to greatly increase the number before
the tad of November, when the next meeting of
the Conciliation Board would be held in Wolver-
hampton, so that the men might then be able to
demand with success terms that should greatly im-
prove the position of the operative. The men
would not, however, be content till the organisa-
tion of the masters as well as the men was national
so that the meetings of the Conciliation Board
which already affected wages everywhere else
might do so officially, masters and men from all
the districts being the legislators.

articles.title: LONDON, OPERATIVE CABINET MAKERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON, OPERATIVE
CABINET MAKERS.

11.....,••••••••

On Wednesday evening a general meeting of
the above trade was held at the Loyal United
Friends' Hall, Banner-street, St. Luke's, to
establish a branch of the Alliance Cabinet Makers'
Association in connection with the fancy cabinet
trade, and to take into consideration the position of
the trade in reference to the 10 per cent. move-
ment.

Mr. Hurry Ham occupied the chair, and after
stating the objects of the meeting, said the most
certain way to obtain their rights was to combine,
for without combination there was always a low
rate of wages. The Alliance Association had
twice obtained an advance of 10 per cent., and it
had reduced the hours of labour five or six hours
a week. If they did not anticipate an advance of
wages they should join the Alliance, for should
there be any dispute the society would take it up
for them.

Mr. Potts said this great question of trades
unions is becoming of vital importance to every
trade, artistic and non-artistic. This movement
was brought about by the Alliance Association
sending a deputation and holding out the right-
hand of fellowship which was graciously accepted
by the fancy cabinet makers. The effect of join-
ing the Association would be the preventing
masters from taking work at too low prices.
When there is a slackness in trade a man is not
forced to work for less money when he can go to
the secretary and get 153. a week.
The speaker proposed that the fancy cabinet
makers should become an affiliated branch or the
Alliance Association.

Mr. Marshall seconded the resolution, which
was carried unanimously.
Mr. Smith, secretary, stated there were 750
members, and that they would soon have 900.
Mr. Hartington expressed his confidence in the
society, and suit the trade ought to have con-
fidence in it. He proposed the following resolu-
tion :

That it was the opinion of this meeting that
they should not debate the question of the 10 per
cent. this evening. •

Mr. Hutchings seconded the resolution, which
w 59 carried. -

After a vote of thanks to the chairman and the
committee of the Alliance Association, proceedings
were closed.

articles.title: LONDON GARMENT DYERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON GARMENT DYERS.

A meeting of tho above trade was held on
Tuesday night at the Cambridge Hall, Newman-
street, Oxford-street, for the purpose of taking
into consideration the advisability of forming a
society, considering the unfavourable result that
had accrued from their want of unity in the
recent agitation for a reduction of hours.

The chair was taken by Air. Ross, who in
opening the proceedings stated that the men had
memorialised the masters to the effect that 561
hours should be recognised throughout the trade,
as a week's work, but at a meeting of masters
held after the memorial had reached them a

resolution was passed, that in their opinion 58
hours would meet the requirements of the trade ;
and he, the Chairman, stated that the Committee,
as representative of the trade, had accepted the
masters' offer simply became they were obliged
to do so, as they vf ere not sufficiently organised to
stand upon their demands; concluding his remarks
by advising those present to form a society for
the protection of their interests.

The secretary, Mr. Page, read the correspond-
ence that had taken place between the masters and
the men, which embraced a resolution arrived at
by the masters, viz., that a week's work should
consist of 58 hours, to terminate at 2 o'clock on
Saturday, and that such 58 hours should be so
divided by each' particular master as to meet the
requirements of his shop.
A resolution to the following effect was moved
by Mr. Snape

That we do form a trade society for the protec-
tion of the interests of garment dyers in the
London district, and more especially with a view
of reducing the number of working hours per
week to 54, and that we elect a committee of
thirteen to draw up and carry out such rules and
regulations as they think most conducive to the
trade in. general.

A great deal of dissent followed this resolution,
and ultimately an amendment was moved to the
effect that the words "fifty-four hours" should
be omitted, which met with the approval of the
mooting, and was carried unanimously.

articles.title: METROPOLITAN POLICE.
articles.text:
THE METROPOLITAN POLICE.

A very large meeting of members of the G and
Y divisions of the Metropolitan police was held
on Wednesday at the Goswell hail, Goswell-
road, for the purpose of considering the questions
of increase of pay, alteration in hours of day duty,
payment when on the sick list owing to injuries
received in the performance of duty, and also with
the view of appointing delegates to attend the
Conference which is proposed to be held imme-
diately, and which has for its object the adoption
of a memorial to the Chief Commissioner, repre-
senting the views of the Metropolitan Police gene-
rally respecting their present position. There were
ilpwards of two hundred police-constables present,
notwithstanding an intimation from one of the
chief officials that the attendance of the men at
the meeting would result in serious consequences
to them, if not to the immediate dismissal of those
taking a prominent part in the proceedings, with-
out any reason being assigned for so extreme a
step.

The meeting has compelled Colonel Henderson
to yield to the pressure of the Police for better pay,
by adopting the course chosen some time ago in
the City, and promising to take the nion's' claims
into earnest consideration. The question of pay—
so the superintendents are instructed to inform
those below them in the force—" will be imme-
diately submitted to the Secretary of State for his
consideration and decision ; " and the Assistant
Commissioner trusts to the "good sense and feel-
ing of the men themselves" to obviate any neces-
sity for prohibiting further meetings On the sub-
ject.

articles.title: NATIONAL AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' UNION.
articles.text:
NATIONAL AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS' UNION.

On Wednesdey, CO delegates, representing nearly
5,000 farm labourers in the Milton district of this
Union, assembled at the Town-hall, Oxford, and
formally affiliated it to the National Union. Mr.
C. Holloway, of Wootton, presided, supported by
Mr. J. Arch, the president of the Union. It was
decided to make Banbury the centre of a separate
district, with 4,000 members. A district committee
and officers were appointel.
In the evening there was a crowded public
meeting at the same place; Mr. R. Reid, of Wor-
cester College, in the chair. The following resolu-
tion was proposed by Mr. U. Taylor, secretary of
the Union, seconded Mr. T. H. Green, of Balliol
College, and carried by acclamation :
That the meeting sympathizas with the agricul-
tural labourers in their present struggle to obtain
their legitimate rights, social and political, and
pledges itself to support them to the utmost.
Mr. Arch proposed the resolution approving of
the affiliation of Oxfordshire to the Natianul Union.
Professor Rogers, in seconding it, spoke of the
avaricious landlords as the primary cause of the
low wages of the labourers. The resolution having
been carried unanimously, the Rev. J. C. Fletcher,
rector of St. Martin's, and the Rev. W. B. Duggan,
vicar of St. Paul's, Oxford, expressed their hearty
sympathy with the movement, as did also Mr, J.
Towle, J.P. The meeting was enthusiastic
.but
somewhat disorderly, owing to interruptions by
undergraduates.

fessors Stubbs, Bernard, and Dr. Pusey got
in. There was also sheen contest among the
candidates from Convocation.

The well-known Servian leader, Mileties,
has contradicted the rumour current on Wed-
nesday that he had been seized by an attack of
apoplexy.

It is stated that the A.ustrian government
will probably despatch Count Beust as Ambas-
sador Extraordinary to be present at the
celebration of the fiftieth anniversary (golden
wedding) of the King of Saxony.

A contemporary is informed that the Com-
mission to be appointed with reference to the
operation of the Factory Acts will be simply a
Commission of Inquiry. It is not improbable
that it will be composed of one or two laymen
and medical men, who will visit the principal
centres of the manufacture of Textile Fabrics,
and report to the Home Secretary before
February next. -

It is said that the Imperial ea 9 Company
Is discussing with the Independent, Commer-
cial, and Ratcliffe Gas Companies the terms of
amalgamation.

• Evin Kennedy, the shepherd injured in the
Kirtlebridge collision, died on Tuesday in
Ptunfries Infltmary. Mr. Reid, of Glasgow,
VMS able to go home, but Mr. Bald, of Coat-
bridge, and Mr. Lamond, of Liverpool, are in
a critical condition.

The sittings of. the Judicial Committee will
be resumed on the sth of November. There
are 45 appeals on the list, and three standing
over for judgment.

Information has- been reeeived from Mani-
toba, by Sir eorge Cartier, of the arrival
there on the 20th inst. of the expedition which
some time since left Canada, 200 strong, under
the command of Lieutenant-Oolonel O. Smith.
The party took about . three weeks to effect
their passage by the Dawson route from the
head of Lake Superior, and arrived at their
destination without casualties.

Additiond accommodation is about to be
provided_ at the Wandsworth and Brookwood
Lunatic Asylums, at a cost to the county of
£73,000,
Etee the corning of the
institution 279 patients have been taken there
"91 'Caterham
from both the above-named hospitals, and
their places are being tilled from private
lioonsed houses. The plans provide further
space for lop males and 300 female 'patients.
At Brookwood and at Wandsworth 51 Single

A singular abuse of official power has been
charged against a policeman, at Stocton- on-
Tees, by the overseer of a wholesale grocery.
The constable, it.is stated, entered the place in
uniform, and began to kiss the girls employed,
and when the foreman remonstrated the in-
vader seized him by the throat and threatened
him with his belt. The offender, who has been
dismissed the force, did not appear in court,
and a warrant was granted to apprehend him.

At the October adjourned Middlesex
Sessions it was stated that the standard of
education among the eighty two prisoners on
the calendar was exceedingly low. A porter
was tried on the charobn of stealing from the
Government stores at Pimlico a pair of boots,
worth ten shillings, "the property of her
Majesty," and Winrr found guilty was recom-
mended to mercy by the jury. It appeared
that the prisoner had been engaged at wort
ten hours a day for sixteen shillings a week,
and the judge, observing that the theft was of
a paltry character, Sentenced bid to aix
Months' hard labour.

At Clerkenwell Police-eourt, Messrs. Payne
and Parker, notorious skittle-sharpers, were
eharged with attempting the fraud known as
" ringing the changes" in a tobacco shop.
Net only did they get more change than they
Ought for money paid for a small purchase, but
it was found that they had carried off packets
of tobacco from nearly every shop at which
that article was sold between the old of
Oxford-street and the Angel, Islington.

According to advices from Odessa, a con-
spiracy has been disoovered in the Caucasus,
and, it is believed, a general rising of all the
Circassian tribes was intended, The leaders
have been imprisoned.

An order appears in Tuesday's Gazette con-
firming the draft scheme of amendments re.
lative to the efficiency of Volunteers which
was laid before Parliament on the 18th of
June, and directing that the sante shall come
into operation on the Ist of November, but so
that the drills of November, 1871, and
November, 1872, shall be reckoned, if need
be, to complete the number of drills needed
for the efficiency of a volunteer for the year
ending 31st October, 1872.

It is said that M. Thiers is preparing a
Message to be delivered to the National
Assembly on its re-assembly after the long
recess. The President is threatened, in the
next meeting of the permanent Commission,
with several questions on the affair of Prince
Napoleon • but he is expected to stay away—
sagaciously leaving the matter in the hands of
the Assembly itself.

M. Ozenne, the negotiator of the new Anglo-
French Treaty of Commerce, has returned to
London—whither he will shortly be followed
by the Comte d'Harcourt. Many reports are
current as to the modifications made in the
old Treaty; but before the official promulga-
tions, it is impossible to say in what precisely
the changes will consist.

According to a telegram received at Rangoon
from/ Promo, the Panthays have been practi-
cally crushed, the road to China is open, and
great rejoicings have taken piace among the
Chinese at Bhatno and Mandalay, who doubt-
less see in the suppression of the rude and
suspicious border people a great prospect of
prosperity for themselves, The news, how-
ever, is probably
tof much more real conse-
quence in its bearing on English communica-
tions with the Far East.

At the Middlesex Sessions; John Harrison,
a dealer in questionable books and prints, of
tight years standing was convicted and
sentenced to two years' imprison went with hard
labour.

Sandringham, with the usual festivities.

It has been arranged that a new bishopric
shall be created for Australia, the seat of wiüh
shall be at Ballarat. By consent, the nomina-
tion of the first Bishop will rest with the
Archbishop of Canterbury.

The Lords of the Admiralty have notified
that they intend to pay their annnal visit of
inspection to Chatham Dockyard to-day(Satur=
day.)

a petition was presented requesting the
Government to enter juts negotiations with
Great Britain, with a view to the cession of
Gibraltar to Spain.

M. Babinet, of the Institute. M. Babinet was

A Public Meeting will be held at the Mansion House,
on Monday, November 4, at Four o'clock in the afternoon.
The Right lion. the Lord Mayor will preside. The
Citizens of London and employers of labour generally,
are invited to attend and help the people to become the
Freeholders of the Alexandra Palace and Park of 500
acres, so that the property may be preserved in its
grand integrity in the interests of public health and pure
recreation.

A Meeting of the People will be held at the Mansion
House, at Seven o'clock in the evening of Monday,
November 4th, under the presidency of the Right lion.
the Lord Mayor, in order that they may themselves
declare their wishes in reference to this movement, and,
by active assistadee, support the efforts which are now
being made to acquire the property in their interest.

people, is invited for the purpose of concerting measures
for helping the Mansion House Committee in this
national work.

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 26, 1872.

THE WELSH LEA.D-MINERS AND
TLIEIR MONTHLY PAYS.
WE desire to express a deep sense of the
service done to the cause of manual labour by
the gentleman who, in the Daily News, gives
the results of his observation and experience.
To this shrewd and honest on-looker Mr. Atm"
and his fellows were indebted for bringing public
sympathy and moral support to their side in
their temperate struggle with the landowners
and farm-tenants of Warwickshire. The sub-
sequent pictures of the state of things among
the miners of Northumberland and Durham
are well-adapted to cheek that ignorant im-
patience of industrial independence and self-
assistance which does so little credit to super-
ficial minds among the sedions of the middle
class. Intelligent readers of his letters from
the North could not fail to receive the impres-
sion that the colliers along the Tyne and the
Wear arc men not to be trifled with; and that,
although the wretched style in which too
many among them are housed by those whom
they enrich, with other unfavourable circum-
stances, tends to the perpetuation of a low
order of moral ideas and of social comfort, they
respond as a class to those Quaker and other
considerate employers who make a conscience
of attending to their just claims, and have, to
a hopeful extent, come under those modiative
principles implanted by WESLEY and his fel-
low helpers in the minds and hearts of their
grandfathers; besides deriving from the
orderly character of the religious institutions
which that goat reformer and eminent friend
to the poor planted in every district where he
obtained influence, uncommonly clear notions
of efficient organization which were sure to be
of service to their whole class whenever occa-
sion should require. It will be so in every
part of the country and in every staple trade,
in proportion to the density of the population
and to the hold which such moral agencies
have taken.
When we brought before our readers the
substance of the evidence taken by the Com-
missioners on the Truck Acts, it appeared, as
will be remembered, that a great deal of the
untheift which so strangely infected even the
Scotch character in the mining and iron dis.

tricts at that end of the island, was laid at the
door, not merely of illegal compulsion to spend
wages in truck, but specially of the employers
as persisting in the unrighteous and demoral-
ising system of long pays. Now, since the
travelling correspondent of the Daily News
passed from the North of England to the North
of Wales, the public learns that, in the Pi in-
cipality, the pay-clays at great works come
round but once a month. When he investi-
gated the state of matters at the slate quarries
of Lord PENRITYN (better known to many per-
sons as Colonel PENNANT), he found the
arrangements awl relations betwixt employer
and employed to be almost everything that
heart would wish or benevolence desire. The
sole, almost only, exception was that, instead
of wages being paid weekly, a whole lunar
month must elapse before the day for handling
coin came round again. By the letter last re-
ceived from the same hand, we find that the
same practice exists among the lead-miners
of Flintshire ; and we may suppose that it
characterises the great works of North Wales
generally.
The Welsh load-miners deserve every con-
sideration from their employers and from the
public. They labour on a mineral and in an
atmosphere more than commonly prejudicial
to health. Even with four shifts during the
four-and-twenty hours, they cannot keep off
that poisonous disease which goes by the
name of the "miners' asthma ;" and yet the
mine owners are represented as bent upon
reducing the number to those of eight hours
each. Candour obliges us to allow that, in
some respects, the men have brought this upon

themselves, and that the large proprietors have
alleviated the morbid pressure by improved ven-
tilation, and by the substitution of descending
and ascending cages for those long ladders which
both strained the muscles and wore out the lungs.
This is the more creditable to the employers,
in that the mines being less productive than
of yore, the earnings made are correspond-
ingly limited. It is also a sign both of im-
provement and of better understanding that
for some years the outside public has ceased
to hear of those callings out of the military to
quell the risings of the minors that discredited
former times. Coal-mining may be as
arduous as lead-mining, and even more so ; yet
it does not follow, as the employers would seem
to argue, that because the Ruabon coal-miners
work eight hours at a stretch, therefore the
Holywell lead-getters should be willing to do

the same. There are other things to be taken
into account besides mere muscular exertion.
The wages of the workers in lead are lower

than those of the workers in coal, a circum-
stance which goes to fortify the credibility of
the men of Flintshiro in pleading that six
hours' work is as much as they can endure
at a spell. The time when they, like diggers
for gold, were stimulated by the prospect of
special gains from independent labour, is a
time gone by. One man hit upon a nugget,
and twenty found nothing. The experiment
had a fair trial; for the masters wanted lead,
and the men paid them double royalty. In
the meantime, the poor follows paid the penalty
of their own ill-provided speculativeness in an
aggravated form of that "miners' asthma,"

from which no pains or provision ()an ever
wholly relieve them. Even the comparatively

few instances of success resembled the conduct
imputed to the native holders of secret silver
mines in Central America, who get some one
when they are hungry, and idle till their neces-
sities return. When they hit upon a lode of
lead, they took out, from time to time, what
met their momentary wants, to make, ere long,
the double discovery, that they had been
living upon their capital, and that it had come
to an end. Upon the whole, therefore, the
old practice of private adventure may be said
to have experienced a similar fate.
It would be interesting and instructive to
compare the social results of lead mining in
South Wales with those of lead mining in
Cumberland and Durham. The miners of the
, London Lead Company in those counties work
' at their own risk, with a yearly settlement
and a monthly allowance from the Company
for ad interim subsistence. The men invest in
land, houses, and savings' bank. The Com-
pany provides schools, and insists upon the
children being sent, This system relates to

a population of over 10,000 souls. At twelve
boys may leave school and wash lead. Mr.
Assistant-Commissioner Foster, in 1858-60,
found the cottages of the lead-miners superior,
in all respects, to those of the colliers. The
pictures and books betokened taste and intelli-
gence, and there was a personal comeliness in
the young which implied good breeding.
Many of the fathers kept both a cow and a
pony. "In this dale," said one of them,
"the uneducated will soon be considered
lunatics."

It did not fall within this gentleman's pro-
vince to trace the effect of the" monthly sub-
sistence money ;" but there is no appearance of
its having had anything like the same effect as
the monthly payment of wages in Flintshire.
The Holywell lead-miner is pictured to us, as
counting to the last penny his monthly receipts,
to see whether it will cover thebalance against
him in the books of the provision-dealer and
the clothier. Most frequently every farthing
has been pledged before paid. lie lives from
hand. to mouth, while the shopkeeper from
whom he takes credit is even buying houses
and land. The County Court is:crowded with
miners summoned for payment of exorbitant
prices through the credit that monthly pays
have obliged them to accept. Nine-tenths of
them live on credit at this pinching and
ruinous rate, and are evermore in the greedy
clutches of the itinerant hucksters. The one-
tenth who escape are men, no doubt, of a supe-
rior type, morally and intellectually ; but, as a
body, the miners have the character of sobriety,
orderliness, cleanliness, and fondness for their
bits of garden. But to this day, the adults
among them are crassly ignorant. This, no
doubt, prevents their seeing the wrong done to
them by monthly pays, and the wrong they do
themselves and their families by submission to
them. And indeed, it greatly concerns the
good name of these noble and ignoble em-
ployers to clear themselves of the imputa-
tion of pocketing a month's interest on every
man's bard earnings.

articles.title: CSN IT BE EXPLAINED?
articles.text:
CSN IT BE EXPLAINED?

In the Times of last Monday, under the
head of" The Iron and Coal Trades," the fol-
lowing words appeared:—" Lord DUDLEY'S
marked bars are firm at £l4 12s. 6d.; the other
leading houses arc asking £l4, but second-
class firms are offering as low as zi2ll 10s. to
£l2. These minimum rates are, however,
nearly double the average standard for bars
during the last ton years."
Let us ask ourselves what this means. The
Times, we presume, is well informed as to its
facts. Possibly Messrs. CREED and WILLIAMS
who a few years since adorned its columns
with fanciful objections to trades unions, on
the ground that these bodies were fast driving
the trade out of the country by raising the
cost of export commodities, are now furnishing
facts like the above as a sly warning to our
ironmasters in reference to the same danger.
If so, it would be very useful if they would
furnish a few additional facts with the view of
giving greater weight to their teaching. We
are puzzled somewhat, and should very much
like to have matters cleared up. For ten
years, we are informed, the average price
of bars was little more than half the minimum
stated. Let us say at a guess it was £7.
Nevertheless ironmasters managed to live, to
struggle on, and save a trifle into the bargain.
The CRIWSIISYS and other great ,ironmasters
had no occasion to send round the hat, nor
even to retire from their mansions or lay down
their carriages. Unquestionably they had a
profit then.
This being the ease, what, we ask, have
they now? Men understanding the business
can tell; why do they not? Making allowance
for the rise in the price of coal and in wages,
there must be still a magnificent margin, which
it would be instructive to explain. Those
diamonds of Lora DUDLEY'S at the recent
Exhibition are not all black diamonds. They
are the sparkling product of iron and coal,
extracted by the alchemy of labour. Why
does not some friend to capital, who is at the
same time an enemy to trades unions, explain
the product? SIDNEY SNIITII or Mr. DUDGEON,
who is so uneasy about the growing power of
the working people, might furnish a few hints
on the subject. If English working men are
so exacting as not to give their employers in

the iron trade a chance of making more than
£6 or £7 a ton on their best bars, they ought
to be superseded by foreign workmen, or
Chinese Coolies, who, by being less trouble-
some, would give their employers a chance of
making larger profits.
The Times, in its impartiality of spirit,
might write an excellent article on this.
There is a danger in it, however, which
should not be overlooked, as in this same
article we ere informed that Belgium and
even France are sending into our markets a
given kind of manufactured iron; and are at
the same time taking large orders at home,
which, in the ordinary course of business,
would have found their way here. If working
men were the cause of this, or if there was
even a shadow of a chance of saying they
were, we should have had columns on columns
of abuse, of indignant protest, of solemn
warning, of argumentative remonstrance.
They would be told how bad it was for the
country; how it would re-act on them-
selves injuriously; how it would drive the
oapital out of the country. Seeing, however,
that the employers are the offenders, there is
no word of abuse, rebuke, or protest. It seems
all perfectly right. The pudding of the em-
ployer is filled with plums, and he is privileged
to go on gorging in peace and quiet. It is
only when the poor man, the vulgar worker,
asks for a miserable mouthful, that our news-
paper press and our respectable people become
alarmed for the welfare of the nation and the
safety of its trade. An extra sixpence a day
for a working man somehow or other strikes at
the very root of society, whilst an extra VI or
£7 a ton profit on bar-iron is as satisfactory
as the fulfilment of the prophecies.

articles.title: POLITICAL ECONOMY AMONGST THE
articles.text:
POLITICAL ECONOMY AMONGST THE

FAMIERS.

THERE can be no promise of good from the
struggle now going on in the agricultural dis-
tricts if it be allowed to degenerate into a class
strife embittered by hatred. So far there has
not been much to complain of. Loose words
have been spoken, and much stupid disquisition
Indulged in by those who ought to have known
bettor; bat the effeet of this has almost entirely
died away; and if those who possess meet in-
fluence for a peaceable settlement will use it
wisely, an understanding may be arrived at
which will be accepted, for a time at least, as
binding on all.
The clergy, who might be active in such a
work as this, seem to be doing nothing; and
what is unusual with them, they have not even
been saying much. So far, therefore, serious
mischief has been avoided; and if no great
advance has been made in the direction of a
permanent settlement, tha breach so far has
not been mischievously widened.
We are afraid this state of things, un-
satisfactory as all thoughtful men must feel
it to be, will, during the coming winter, alter
for the worse rather than for the better. The
short sharp days of winter arc greatly in
favour of the farmer, if he feel disposed to
take advantagedf the power they will give him;
and it is discouraging to notice that the in ten-
tion to do so has been unpleasantly in anifesting
itself. The account given in the newspapers a
few days since of a farmers' meeting at New-
market, in consequence of a demand made on
them by the labourers, is anything but en-
couraging. Of course, the farmers have a
perfect right to unite and to resist the labourers'
demands. This is freely granted; but when
they go beyond this, and declare by resolution
that one of the objects of their association is
to 1i a maximum price for labour, they do
not only what is ridiculous but highly
dangerous into the bargain; dangerous because
it is an evidence of folly which,, manifested
in other directions, may hurry matters into
riot and disorder. If working men of
any class had committed, such a blunder,
they would have been assailed from, all
quarters ; their ignorance would have been
rebuked in the strongest language; but the
farmers, so far as we have seen, have not had it
anywhere pointed out to them how very wrongly
they have acted. It is true that trades unions,
as sellers of labour, flx. where they can a
minimum price; but the right to do . thia
cannot be denied to the sellers of any com-
tnedity, whether they stand 'singly or in

assoCiation. Bat working men never any-
where, as buyers of any commodity, sought to
lay down the maximum price the seller should
charge for it.
A committee of old women managing an
association with the object of not allowing
the butcher to charge more than sixpence
a pound for his beef, would be laughed
at; or a society of children declaring
that lolly-pops should not go above a half-
penny an ounce, would deserve whipping and
sending to school for the purpose of studying
the rudiments of political economy. But
whatever there might be of the ludicrous in
such things they would be harmless, as the
butchers would laugh at the old women,
whilst the sweetstuff people would turn the
children out of their shops. But associated
farmers, fixing the maximum price for labour,
not on dangerous ground. The conflicts likely
to arise under such circumstances may be as
violent on the one side as they are stupid and
absurd on the other. If sneh an act gives
the measure of our farmers' intelligence, what
are we to expect from the men? or what can
we look for from a contest entered upon by men,
knowing nothing of the principles by which
their conduct in relation to each other should
be regulated, and feeling at the same time,
mutual anger, distrust, and hatred, in conse-
quence of their opposition to each other? Our
press ought to undertake the teaching of the
A B C of politioal economy to the farmers—
that is, if they know anything about it.
Failing this, the great trades unions ought
to set up a professorship, and try to get
the middle and upper-class people to under-
stand that the general laws of this much
talked of, hut little understood, science apply
to all classes and interest alike, and are meant
to produce justice in employers, as well as to
regulate reasonably the conduct of working
men. A new and vigorous teaching is, no
doubt, needed, if we are to prevent self-willed
people from producing very disagreeable social
and industrial entanglements.

articles.title: COAITE DE CHAMBORD.
articles.text:
COAITE DE CHAMBORD.

IT is difficult to read the letter of the Count
DE CITAMBORD to M. DE LA. ROCIIETTP, without
some degree of pity for the unhappy man who
penned it. A King by Right Divine without
a crown to put on his head or a throne to sit
on must feel even more uncomfortable than an
ordinary mortal without shoes and stockings
to his feet, or a hat to his head. And, what is
worse, France, to which he looks as his natural
inheritance, seems every day more and more
disposed to do without him or any person
with like claims on her.

In this letter he declares France to be, at
bottom, "Catholic and monarchical." He
had not the prudence to wait till Sunday's
elections were over; and now that he is in
print the declaration of France, so far as she
has spoken, falsifies his statement.
As a matter of course, he makes the old
charges against the Republicans who oppose
him. Those who support his pretensions are
good people, and those who do not are bad.
people—the old child's complaint. He is really
the true Simon Pure; only, somehow or other,
people don't care about him. It is a pity,
perhaps, but how can such a state of things
be altered ? France wants repose; and he
thinks he could help her to that blessing, but
the people will not listen to his lullaby. If men
but wished for their " true " good, he imagines
they would bring him back. But he forgets
that they sought for their "true good" in that
way once before, and did not find it.

We imagine that in France, in this hour,
people are looking for their true good in quite
a different direction. They have to ohoose
between three sets of pretenders and govern-
ment of themselves by themselves, and it
looks at present as if they were about to prefer
themselves. If they would make their minds
UP to give the world unmistakable proof of
this, and treat with wholesome severity those
who interfered with them by dynastic intrigues
and conspiracies, they would soon set the
question at rest; and if, in addition, they
would take the education of the young out of
the hands of the priests, they would settle for
ever a question which will never cease to dis-
tract them till they have done so. Nations are
made or saved by decidedovise, and courageous

policies; but France has not yet clearly shown
that she possesses a policy characterised by any
one of these high attributes.

THE AIORLEY COAL-PIT EXPLOSION.

TRE inquest on the bodies of the thirty-two
men and boys killed at Morley, near Leeds,
by the coal-pit explosion, has terminated in a
verdict attributing the catasthrope mainly to
the carelessness of those whose duty it was to
see to the proper ventilation of the mine.
Mr. WARML, the Government inspector,
condemned the loose discipline of the colliery.
The explosion had been caused by the gas from
the goals, which was not properly ventilated,
coming in contact with the lights in the in-
take airway, and not from the use of a match
or fuzee by one of the men. He suggested
certain improvements in the mode of ventila-
tion, notably the disuse of furnaces, and the
substitution of fans. In answer to Mr. GILL,
who represented the owners, he said they had
hitherto carried out every improvement he had
suggested.

articles.title: NEW LORD CHANCELLOR.
articles.text:
THE NEW LORD CHANCELLOR.

THE first subject on which Lord SELBORNE
(Sir ROWIDELL PALMER) has opened his mouth
since being made Lord Chancellor is the union
of all classes in one fellowship. We accept
this as a good omen, and that the more readily
because the speaker is known to be a sincere,
earnest, and conscientious man.
"For the whole country," (he said on the open-
ing es his new house at Selborre) "I desire
nothing so much, or more heartily pray God for, as
that all classes of the people may be united in the
bands of brotherly love one with another, that those
who, by the accident of fortune, or by the provi-
dence of God—which is the more proper expression
—have in any way been raised to a position of
apparent advantage over others, may not be
exalted by those outward distinctions, but may be
brought more and more to see that their truest
happiness will lie in cultivating those relations of
brotherhood which are their real relations with
those who are in some degree below thorn in the
walk of life ; and that those who arc less gifted
with outward or worldly advantages, may not
suffer any evil disposed or designing person to stir
them up to think that their happiness and welfare
would be promoted by attempting to subvert the
established order of society, or to undo those laws
which God has established for the government of
the world; but that all may know that by each
man faithfully, providently, and as in the sight of
God, doing his proper work, he will boat raise his
class and render himself a happy man and a good
citizen. I desire that the bonds of love may more
and more prevail between high and low, rich and
poor, one with another.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' UNION.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS'
UNION.

Tan Agricultural Labourers' Union makes
progress. A meeting was held at Oxford on
Wednesday, which possesses interesting
features. Though the ptoceedings were a
little interrupted by some thoughtless under-
graduates of the University, a friendly part
was taken in them by clergymen, professors,
and graduates. On the same platform, and
engaged in the same work, were JOSEPH ARCH,
Professor ROGEIIS, gentlemen belonging to two
principal colleges, and two incumbents of
Oxford parishes. Such was the meeting at
which it was resolved :

That the meeting sympathises with the agricul-
tural labourers in their present struggle to obtain
their legitimate rights, social and political, and
pledges itself to support them to the utmost.

articles.title: ALEXANDRA PARK AND PALACE.
articles.text:
THE ALEXANDRA PARK AND
PALACE.

Nothing can be more clear and satisfactory than
the prospect existing that the unrivalled resources
of this magnificent domain will shortly be developed
for the best of all purposes to which they could be
applied. Lest the following paragraph should
have escaped the notice of those of our readers who
are not in the meritorious habit of scanning every
paragraph in the morning papers, we reproduce it
from the Times of the 11th inst.

"The Mansion House Committee on the
Alexandra Park met to-day (Thursday) to
receive from the Lord Mayor the re-
sult of his negotiations with, the owners of
the property. It was explained that when the
vendors can be assured that £lOO,OOO will be
forthcoming they will enter into a contract for
sale, and the Lord Mayor proposed to comply
with this condition by means of a guarantee
fund, precisely similar to that by which the great
Exhibition of 1851 was carried out. He ex-
plained that he was in possession of information
from the representatives of skilled artisans and
others—not only in London, but in Manchester,
Birmingham, Liverpool, and elsewhere—which
left no doubt on his mind that the whole of the
purchass-money will be provided by them, and
that he, therefore, could invite his friends to fol-
low his example and sign the deeds for £l,OOO.
The guarantee was then, in addition, numerously
signed by the Committee, and left for further sig-
natures at the Mansion House."

Carrying the pleasing narrative t) our day of
publication, we learn that the subscription has
progressed as favourably as could be expected at
a time when so many are still "out of town."
We think it not improbable that, on the return of
the absentees, they will find the indispensable
preliminary conditions of the contract completed.
For the credit and honour of the good and
wealthy, we trust that the guarantee will be
promptly filled. It is scarcely possible to suppose
otherwise. When we reflect upon what has taken
place in provincial boroughs, where the successful
merchant or manufacturer has contributed his
thousands, his five, his ten, his thirty thousands,
in order to secure for his bumbler neighbours the
blessing of an open park and exercise-ground, we
cannot imagine that in London, the great centre
of opulence and benevolence, there will be any
backwardness in doing all that is necessary to
enable our workers to oktin for themselves so
splendid a possession as the Park and Palace. The
Lord Mayor has assured us, to his own knowledge,
that the people are willing and anxious to do their
part. We should not think it possible that the
Lord Mayor would be now deserted, at the crisis
of his admirable labours, even if subscription to
the guarantee involved the final contribution of
the sums subscribed for. How improbable, then
is it that there should be hesitation, when the
practical certainty is that the guarantee fund will
be merely a formal one!
In the meantime it is pleasing to hear of the
spirit manifested by the working classes them-
selves. Not only front London, but from various
large towns and centres of industry, the Lord
Mayor has received authorized assurances of the
determination of the "working-bees" to do all
that their friends expect of them, and to purchase
the Park and Palace for themselves. His wise
and generous action is, it is said, appreciated by
those whom he desires to serve. If so, considering
their vast numbers, and the prosperity which has
for some time been enjoyed in most of the great
departments of business, it will be strange if, on
time being allowed them, the whole amount
required is not forthcoming from those whose
interests are most deeply concerned in the success
of the object to which it is to be devoted. Their
representative and leading men cannot better prove
a faithful inclination to do them good than by
exhorting thorn to support a movement so emphati-
cally identified with benefit to themselves.

It is only fair to add that they are doing so.
The Executive Committee, appointed for the pur-

OCT. '26, 1872

THE EAST LONDON MUSEUM.

A. complimentary banquet was given on
Tuesday evening at the London Tavern to Sir
Antonio Brady, the Rev. S. Hansard, Dr.
Millar, and Mr. Clubon, for the exertions in
promoting the East London Museum, which is
achieving such a Success at Bethnal-green.
About a hundred gentlemen sat down to table
under the presidency of Mr. T. F. Bradbrook,
the senior churchwarden of Bethnal-green.
The 'chairman, in giving the usual loyal
toasts, expressed the satisfaction, of the East-.
end of Loudon that the Prince and Princess of
Walei had been present, at the opening et the
Museum, and expressed the belief that the
reception they had met with on that motion
mist •'.haVe satisfied every one that the East-
end of the metropolis was as loyal as the West.
Mr. E. 11. Currie proposed "The House of
Ccinninens," and associated with, the toast the
name of Mr. C. Reed, M.P.

said that'the present House of Conanions had
always aVinced the greatest desire to give 'the.
finishing.stioke to the East London Museum
under the circumstances, those circumstances
having been decided upon years before. In
the East of London they regarded the opening

The chairman, in complimentary; terms,

was amply deinoustrated, at the Exhibition of.
1851. After that year foreigners were put on
their metal. The Germans established eleven
universities and,hundreds of technical schools.
What was the result? At the Exhibition of
1862 they trod close upon our heels, and, in
some cases, excelled us. • In softie' instances
they were working up our raw materials and
underselling 114 in our own markets. ,The
East Londoners were not satisfied' With what
they had got it the Bethnal Green. Museum.
Yet in spite of the incompleteness of their

the ,e}overnment contribution of the food

Dr. Millar returned thanks, and then

who had raised a standard which no Govern-
ment would, in the future, ever 'dare to go

Must have further contributions from the

articles.text:
THE AGRICULTUItA.T LABOURERS
AND PARISH RELIEF.

Mr. George Mitchell desires us to publish the
following, which has been forwarded to him :
Sir,—Allow me, as a friend, to offer you one
word of condolence on your loss. Although
living at a great distance from you, I have
need of your sympathy and untiring per-
severance on behalf of the west country agri-
oulttiral labourers' that I determined to meet
you at one of the labourers' meetings, held at
13ridport this past summer, and which con-
vinced me of your earnestness in their cause.
I sincerely trust that kind. Providence will
still continue to smile on you and yours, and
that your great loss will not be felt so severely
as to prevent you from continuing your praise-
worthy work on behalf of those poor, deluded,
ignorant, and half-starved people who inhabit
this part of the nation.
I, myself, do take a deep interest in the poor
creatures, and living as I do amongst them,
it enables me to speak perhaps more positively
than many others as to their wants, and still
more SQ as one of their so-called guardians.
The Axminster Union, in which I am
located, is composed of seventeen parishes, and
I believe there is not half-a-dozen labourers or
any one member Of their family to be found in
the whole seventeen parishes that are not
paupers. The adults are paid for their labour
from 4s. to 10s. per week, and I am afraid so
long as the present poor-law is in existence we
shall not see their condition bettered, nearly
half of the rates that are collected being
appropriated under the present system to the
parsons, doctors, lawyers, and other officials.
The local union boards are composed prin-
cipally of farmers and their landlords, ex-
officio members, which accounts for out-door
relief being paid and received in consideration
of wages.
I must tell you how pauperism is on the
increase in this neighbourhood. At our last
board meeting, held at Axminster on Thurs..
day, 17th inst., application was made by a.
farmer's wife for out-door relief for 'her son,
who lived at home with his parents, who
farmed over 120 acres of land, well stocked,
thus showing you that farmers have little or no
more. pride or independence in them than their
labourers, and they argue in their ignorance
that they have paid poor-rates for years and
never once received back a penny in any other
way than by reduced wages. I endeavour to
instil on tha ratepayers the necessity of pro-
curing education and better remuneration for
;he labourer's work;and by so doing we should
men pauperism and relieve ourselves from
,eavy rates.—Yours,

JOlll4 Dirratut.
Lyme Regis, 21st Ocitober, 1872.

A number of pensioners from the Royal
Arsenal at Woolwich are preparing for a
voyage to Canada and back, in order, as it is
stated, that they may obtain a commutation of
their pensions.

The debate on the subject of gratuitous
education to destitute children was resumed
at the weekly meeting of the School Board of
London on Wednesday, and after several
members had spoken, Par. Reed, M.P., with-
drew his motion in favour of Mr. Pioton's
amendment, which, he said, would open up the
whole question. Mr. Pieton, however, altered
his amendment so as to make it declare that the
Board will consider each ease sent up by the
Divisional Committee on its merits. To this
another
_a.menatncnt was Moved by Lord Ma -
hen, afartning that the necessity of establish-
ing free instruction has not yet arrived.
Eventually Mr. Picton'ilinoticia was carried by
17 to 6. -

Mr. Stanley, the discoverer of Livingstone,
arrived at Glasgow on Wednesday, au tt was
entertained at luncheon by the Lord Provost
and magistrates. He afterwards gave a lecture
to the Christian Young Mon's Association, on
Central Africa.

The herds of deer running in the Home-
park, Hampton Court, are, it is stated, affected
with foot and mouth disease. ,

Owing to the great rainfall of the last few
days, the Trent and Derwent and. other
streams in the Midland Counties have over-
flowed their banks, and the waters have risen
higher than during the greatfloods of 1857 and
1864.

From Oldham we hear of a suicide under
what might have seemed perfectly respectable
and "safe." conditions of life. Mr. J. D.
Worthington, of Collier House—a Wesley.an
in religion, two of whose brothers were maps-
trates—vtas found in his bath, with throat
out, and other wounds on the body lie had
been in low spirits for some time, from some
house not stated, and the verdict was ono of
"temporary insanity."

The Ladies' Medical College, it is stated,
will hereafter be designated "the Obstetrical
College for Women.' It is intended to apply
to Parliament for power to confer on women
a registerable diploma in midwirety, and in the
meanwhile the Female Medical Society has
determined to issue certificates of proficiency
in that branch of the medical art.

At a meeting of the Southwark Liberal
Registration Association, it was stated that
the result of the recent revision of votes was
a net Liberal gain of 295.

A woman, named Hannah Harwood, who
lived with Henry. Linton, a carpenter, in the
basement of the house, No. 32, Hereford-street,
Lisson-grove, was found dead under mys-
terious circumstances on Tuesday afternoon.
Her daughter, on going to see her, found her
lying on the bed undressed, and she had
apparently been dead two or three days.
Linton, who had been met by the daughter on
her coming to the house, was afterwards found,
in another room with his throat cut. lle was
alive, and was taken. to St. Mary's Hospital,
where he lies in a precarious state. He denies
having been the cause of the death of the
, woman, and says he never touched her.

The inquest touehing the death of Ellen
Moore' alias Mary Jane Addington, who was
shot at 9, Northport-street, Hoxton, on the
lath September, was held on Wednesday, and
resulted in a verdict of "Wilful murder"
against Augustus Elliot, who was committed
to take his trial,

The Queen has addressed an autograph letter
to the Earl of Shaftesbury, expressive of her
deep and touching sympathy with him in the
loss he has sustained by the death of the
Countess.

The Prince of Wales ie a 'hit to the Earl
of Aylesford, at Paokirtgton Eall, near
Coventry. •

A series of festivities have taken .place at
&thorn° connected with the completion of
Blaokmoor House, the now mansion of the
Lord Chancellor, and these were brought to a
close on Monday by a dinner given by him, in
the school-room of the parish, to the smaller
tenantry, the artificers, the ringers, choristers,
and other officials of the parish church. Lord
Belborne presided, and made a speech, in
which he dilated on the duty of the higher
classes to cultivate good relations with those
below them in life.

Mr. Tennyson's new poem—the last- of the
Idylls of the King—has just been pulllished.
It bears the name of " Gareth and Lynette,"
and takes a place just after the poem which
tells of the coming of Arthur. Appended to
the new work, is the Idyll of " The Last
Tournament," recording "the in of Tristram
and Isolt;" it appeared in a magazine some
time ago,

Diplornatie complication with Turkey seems
likely to arise out of the intended abolition of
convents in Italy. A note, protesting on
behalf of Eastern religious communities, has
been presented a genie by the Turkish
Legation.

FRIDAY.
The plain silk hands employed by Messrs.
Morley and Co., of Heanor, Devonshire, are
agitating for a considerable advance of wages,
and unless their demand is conceded a strike

will probably nsue.
The inquest on the bodies of Hewitt and
Broadbent, who. were killed in the 'Woodhouse
_

Junction collision' was resumed yesterday
morning before the Deputy Coroner for

Sheffield.

It is rumoured that the Prince of Wales
and Lord StraAhnairn are to be made field-

marshals, the list having been reduced by

recent deaths-.

Typhoid and gastric fever has increased
alarmingly at Wesharn, a village ad.ioining
Kirkham, near Preston. The disease is said

to be attiibutple to preventable causes, and
vigorous action is about to be taken by the

Alfred , Louis Beauvier, a French notary,
has been arrested nit Jersey on accusations of
forgery and fraudulent bankruptcy, for which
he had been condemned in France par con-
tumace. He is charged with having com-
mitted 64 distinct cases of forgery for sums

Cathedral, Dublin, when full choral service

Limoy, the Mayor of Florence, the Prefect,

garrison and of the National Guard, the
foreign consuls, and a large crowd of persons.

horses from Canada.

to the raids committed by the Mexicans on
the American frontier.

work in the Middlesborough district met on

resolutions in favour of a complete amnesty
for the Fenian prisoners. Mr. Martin, M.P.,

wrote to say that English writers, in all de-
partments of literature, as well as other

exceptions, seemed to be in a conspiracy

men.

(Saturday) to consider whether they should
apply to Parliament for power to emstruot
gas works of their own for the supply of, gas
to the city.
The railway service between Nice and
Genoa is interrupted in oonsequence of two
bridges at Savona having been broken down.

France for setting the Maine of the fourth
arrondissement on fire for murder, worn-
pitnied by theft, and for participation in the
Communist insurrection.

at Chelmsford in trying a young woman,
named Ellen Day Kettle, for. the wilful murder

being the former wife of the prisoner's husband.

yesterday without making any change in the
rate of discount.

San Juan boundary question declares that the
claims of the United States fully accord with
, the true interpretation of the Treaty of 16th
June 1846, and that the boundary line has,
therefore, to run through the Hare Channel.
Amongst the first acts of the new Lord
Chancellor was a note to the Rev. Dr. Dyne,'
Head laster of the High School, Highgate,
demanding a half-holiday for the boys. Sir
Roundel' Palmer is one of the governors of

I was at the time of my story, a young °Meer

brunt of the earlier part of the war in the ,Penin-
